summary.text: Half-life is the time required for a quantity to reduce to half of its initial value.
In nuclear physics it describes how quickly unstable atoms decay, and a single radioactive atom has a 50% probability of decaying within its half-life.
When many identical atoms decay, it is a very good approximation to say that half of them remain after one half-life.

facts.label: Its opposite
facts.value: Doubling time, which grows by a factor of 2

facts.label: Constant over time
facts.value: The half-life stays the same as an exponentially decaying quantity shrinks

facts.label: Rock dating
facts.value: Rutherford timed radium's decay to lead-206 to age rocks

facts.label: Water in a person
facts.value: A biological half-life of about 9 to 10 days

items.prompt: One radioactive atom has a half-life of one second. One second goes by. What is true of it?

options.label: Half of the atom has decayed and half remains
It has certainly decayed by now
It had a 50% probability of decaying in that time
It will decay in exactly one more second

items.explain: There is no 'half an atom' left; half-life is defined in terms of probability, and the chance of an atom decaying within its half-life is 50%.

items.prompt: In a simulation with a few identical atoms, the count left after one half-life is not exactly half. What makes 'half remain' a better approximation?

options.label: Starting with a far larger number of atoms
Waiting twice as long before counting
Cooling the atoms before the test begins
Using atoms that are heavier than the first ones

items.explain: Decay has random variation, but with many identical atoms the law of large numbers makes half remaining a very good approximation.

items.prompt: A decaying isotope sample takes a certain time to fall from its full amount to half. How long will the fall from half to a quarter take?

options.label: Half as long, because there is less left to decay
Twice as long, because the decay is slowing down
Four times as long, since the amount has been halved twice
The same time, because the half-life is constant

items.explain: Half-life is constant over the lifetime of an exponentially decaying quantity, so each halving takes the same time.

items.prompt: A pharmacist says a drug has a biological half-life. What does that measure?

options.label: How long the drug takes before it starts to work
How long the body takes to lose half of its activity
How long the body takes to clear the whole dose
How long the drug takes to double its effect

items.explain: A biological half-life is the time it takes for a substance to lose one-half of its pharmacologic, physiologic or radiological activity.

items.prompt: Why is a body's elimination of a substance usually less tidy than a radioactive isotope's decay?

options.label: Isotopes are far larger than the substances a body clears
A living body works on a fixed schedule that isotopes lack
A living organism usually follows more complex kinetics than an isotope does
Isotopes decay only when no living thing is nearby

items.explain: A radioactive isotope decays almost perfectly according to first-order kinetics with a fixed rate constant, while elimination from a living organism usually follows more complex chemical kinetics.

items.prompt: Rutherford used a radioactive element's half-life to answer what question about rocks?

options.label: How old they are
How hot they were when they formed
How much they weigh in total
Which minerals they contain most of

items.explain: Rutherford applied the half-life principle to age determination of rocks, measuring the decay period of radium to lead-206.

paragraphs.heading: What it means
paragraphs.text: A half-life, written t_½, is the time it takes for an amount of something to drop to half of what it started at. The word is common in nuclear physics, where it describes how fast unstable atoms decay. It is also used for any exponential decay, and occasionally for decay that is not exponential. Medicine, for instance, talks about the biological half-life of drugs and other chemicals inside the human body.

paragraphs.heading: A steady clock
paragraphs.text: For a quantity that shrinks exponentially, the half-life stays the same the whole time. Its mirror image is doubling time, which measures growth by a factor of 2 instead of shrinking by it. Ernest Rutherford discovered the principle in 1907 and called it the half-life period, a name cut down to half-life in the early 1950s. He used it to work out the ages of rocks, by measuring the decay of radium to lead-206.

paragraphs.heading: A matter of chance
paragraphs.text: Radioactive atoms come as separate units, which causes a problem. If you have one atom with a half-life of one second, you will not find half an atom after a second. So the half-life is defined by probability: it is the time in which exactly half the atoms decay on average. Put another way, each atom has a 50% chance of decaying within one half-life. With many identical atoms, the law of large numbers makes half remaining a very good approximation, and flipping coins can act this out.

paragraphs.heading: The decay constant
paragraphs.text: The half-life is tied to a second number, the decay constant λ, which is always positive. The link is t_(1/2) = (ln (2))/λ, where ln(2), the natural logarithm of 2, is about 0.693. For radioactive atoms, the half-life depends on the type of atom and isotope. It is usually found by experiment.

paragraphs.heading: In chemical reactions
paragraphs.text: In chemistry, the half-life of a substance is the time for its concentration to fall to half its starting value. In a first order reaction, the rate is proportional to how much reactant there is, so the concentration falls exponentially. Its half-life, t_(1/2) = (ln 2)/k, depends only on the rate constant k and not on the starting concentration. In a zero order reaction, the rate does not depend on concentration, which falls in a straight line, and the half-life does depend on the starting concentration.

paragraphs.heading: In the body and beyond
paragraphs.text: A biological half-life is the time a substance, such as a drug or a radioactive nuclide, takes to lose half of its pharmacologic, physiologic or radiological activity. Clearing a substance from a living body usually follows more complex kinetics than radioactive decay does. The biological half-life of water in a person is about 9 to 10 days, though behavior and other conditions can change it, and for caesium it is one to four months. Epidemiologists use the idea too, for the time it takes the number of new cases in an outbreak to halve.
